newsitem.title: USA: US still committed to protecting Kurds-Pelletreau.
newsitem.headline: US still committed to protecting Kurds-Pelletreau.

text.p: United States assistant secretary of state for Near East affairs, Robert Pelletreau, said on Monday that the U.S. remains committed to protecting Kurds in northern Iraq even though that effort was hampered by the recent action of the Kurdish Democratic Party.

Pelletreau also said that the implementation of the United Nations oil-for-food deal in Iraq would not be held up by the U.S. and could be implemented in a matter of weeks, but said it depended on the security situation in the Kurdish provinces in the north and an agreement between the rival factions there.

The assistant secretary was asked to clarify comments made to Congress last week when he said that protecting the Kurdish enclave "has not been the policy of this administration," a statement which Kurdish leaders said was surprising given the U.S. military protection for no-fly zones in the region for the past five years.

Pelletreau, attending a symposium on Middle East business prospects, said Monday: "We are committed to the Kurds (but) we frankly can't protect the Kurdish leader against Iraq if he invites Iraq in," referring to KDP leader Massoud Barzani.
Barzani allowed Baghdad's troops into the region last month to help him take the Kurdish city of Arbil from rival faction the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
"We are certainly interested in providing humanitarian assistance to them and continuing with the coalition of air support over the north," he added.
Pelletreau said that he had been on the phone with leaders of both groups in an effort to facilitate talks but added that it appears to be too soon after the fighting for that process to begin.

Meanwhile, Pelletreau said that "the U.S. has no intention of delaying implementation of the U.N. oil-for-food deal...(but) it depends on the security situation in northern Iraq" and whether the U.N. monitors will be safe.
Implementation of the oil deal could proceed quickly if the two rival Kurdish sides resolved their differences.
"We are trying to resolve their problems politically and to restore a situation in northern Iraq that would permit resolution 986 to go forward," said Pelletreau.

U.N. resolution 986 allows for $2 billion of oil exports by Iraq over six months, on a renewable basis, for humanitarian relief for ordinary Iraqis, including a portion set aside especially for the Kurds.
"That could come together relatively quickly...in a matter of weeks...if the Kurdish factions can come to an agreement," he said.

Implementation of the deal was suspended by the United Nations last month after Baghdad's intervention on the side of the KDP. The United Nations also said the deal could be restarted soon if the security situation allows, though it has not mentioned the need for an agreement between the two sides.
